title: Time Series Forecasting Through the Lens of Dynamics
claim: Forecasting models decompose into preprocessing, a single dynamics block bridging past to future, and postprocessing, with dynamics location mattering.
layout: Single panel, top-left to bottom-right, time axis at left, dash-dotted past/future divider
description: A single schematic of a time series forecasting model M_theta drawn as a large rounded rectangle. A vertical time axis on the left runs downward (t), split by a horizontal dash-dotted line into a past zone T_X above and a future zone T_Y below. Inside the box, input X flows by a horizontal arrow through a light-blue rounded box f^pre to X_pre. A vertical arrow then goes down through an orange circle f^dyn, which sits on the dash-dotted line and so marks the crossing from past to future, to Y-tilde. From there a horizontal arrow through a second blue box f^post leads to the output Y-hat. Blue boxes mark PRO functions and the orange circle marks the DYN function. The eye goes first to the orange circle and the large math symbols.
caption: PRO and DYN functions illustrated in the processing chain of a TSF model $\mathcal{M}_{\theta}$ where "$\mathcal{T}_X$ before $\mathcal{T}_Y$". PRO functions are framed and blue while DYN function is encircled and orange. Solid lines represent the main data flow. Skip connections are not drawn for better clarity.
abstract: While deep learning is facing an homogenization across modalities led by Transformers, they are still challenged by shallow linear models in the time series forecasting task. Our hypothesis is that models should learn a direct link from past to future data points, which we identify as a learning dynamics capability. We develop an original $\texttt{PRO-DYN}$ nomenclature to analyze existing models through the lens of dynamics. Two observations thus emerge: $\textbf{1.}$ under-performing architectures learn dynamics at most partially, $\textbf{2.}$ the location of the dynamics block at the model end is of prime importance. Our systemic and empirical studies both confirm our observations on a set of performance-varying models with diverse backbones. We propose a simple plug-and-play methodology guiding model designs and improvements.
